title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning guidance, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, recommended operational tooling, and canonical runbooks used by Redwood Inference SRE and Platform teams. It is intended as the primary reference for owners and on-call responders for inference services (hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments).

Goals
- Provide consistent SLI/SLO definitions across inference surfaces (text generation, chat, embeddings, streaming).
- Define actionable error budget policies and escalation triggers.
- Standardize capacity planning cadence and headroom targets.
- Describe reliability initiative lifecycle and prioritization.
- Ensure incident reviews are thorough, timely, and lead to measurable remediation.
- Maintain concise, executable runbooks for common failure modes.

1) SLI and SLO definitions

Summary table (service categories):

Service | Primary SLI | Measurement window | Target SLO
Hosted API (generate/chat) | Successful responses with latency <= p99 threshold | Monthly (30d) | 99.95% availability + p99 latency SLA
Embeddings API | Successful 200 responses + correctness (checksum) | Monthly (30d) | 99.99% availability
Dedicated Pool (customer reserved) | Request success rate & quota compliance | Monthly (30d) | 99.9% availability (contracted)
Control Plane (control APIs, rollout API) | API success rate | 30d | 99.9%

Recommended SLI measurement details:
- Success criteria: HTTP 2xx with non-empty body (and for streaming, final chunk status OK).
- Latency SLI: measured end-to-end at the ingress gateway. Primary quantiles: p50, p95, p99, p99.9.
- Error classification: client errors (4xx) excluded from availability SLO unless caused by platform-side validation regressions; server errors (5xx), timeouts, stream truncation count as failures.
- Synthetic checks: globally distributed synthetic requests every 30s per region for production models; used for alerting and black-box SLO sanity checks.

SLO examples (concrete):
- Hosted Generate API availability: 99.95% successful within latency threshold p99 <= 400ms over 30 days.
- Streaming chat: 99.9% stream continuity (no truncation) over 30 days.
- Embeddings: 99.99% successful responses over 30 days.
- Model upload/rollout API: 99.5% success over 30 days.

2) Error budget policy and burn controls

Definitions:
- Error budget = 1 - SLO. For a 99.95% SLO, monthly error budget = 0.05% of requests.
- Burn rate = observed error fraction / allowed error fraction per rolling window.

Operational thresholds (rolling 7-day and 1-day windows):
- Normal: burn rate < 1.0 - no action required beyond normal monitoring.
- Watch: burn rate 1.0 - 2.0 for 1 day - SRE lead notified; investigate for root causes; convene cross-functional triage if root cause not obvious within 2 hours.
- Restrict: burn rate > 2.0 for 1 day OR cumulative error budget depletion > 50% - pause low-priority rollouts, enable conservative routing (route to stable model variants), and notify customer-facing teams.
- Emergency: burn rate > 5.0 OR error budget exhausted - declare reliability incident; follow incident runbook; SRE, product, and sales leadership notified; executive RCA to be scheduled.

Controls and automated mitigations:
- Canary gating: model rollouts cannot exceed 10% of production traffic until 24h canary passes SLO checkpoints.
- Automated fallback: if availability or latency SLOs breach threshold, traffic routing automatically shifts to pre-approved fallback model or region.
- Rollback policy: any rollout that contributes >25% of incremental error rate must be rolled back within 2 hours of detection.

3) Capacity planning standards

Cadence and ownership:
- Quarterly capacity review led by Eng-SRE with input from Product, Sales (forecasted enterprise commitments), and Eng-Infra.
- Monthly operational capacity sync for near-term adjustments (next 30 days).

Key metrics to track:
- Peak QPS (1-minute and 5-minute windows) by region and by model family.
- 95th and 99th percentile request size (tokens) and request duration distributions.
- GPU utilization, memory headroom, NVME throughput, and host-level CPU.
- Forecasted growth (3-, 6-, 12-month) with confidence bands.
- Reserved capacity commitments (Dedicated customers) vs observed usage.

Headroom and scaling targets:
- Production pools should maintain 30% steady-state headroom on critical resources (GPU memory, GPU SM utilization, host CPU) to tolerate traffic spikes and scheduling churn.
- Autoscaler target: maintain p95 latency below SLO target with autoscaling cooldown <= 90s for burstable services.
- Warm spare capacity: maintain minimum of 1.5x capacity for regional failover scenarios when SLA commitments require regional redundancy.

Capacity planning checklist (monthly):
1. Collect telemetry: QPS by route/model, error rates, latencies, instance counts.
2. Compare against forecasts and reserved commitments.
3. Project shortfall and schedule procurement (cloud/GPU) or reconfigure pools.
4. Validate failover and autoscaling policies in staging (monthly game-day).
5. Publish capacity summary to Eng-SRE dashboard and product stakeholders.

4) Reliability initiatives (RIs) lifecycle

Purpose: Group larger technical work that reduces error budget burn, improves latency tails, or materially reduces operational toil.

RI process:
- Proposal: owner creates an RI page with problem statement, hypothesis, metrics (guardrail SLOs), and rollout plan.
- Review: Eng-SRE prioritizes RIs during quarterly planning with Product and Platform.
- Implementation: small incremental deploys with feature flags and monitoring for regressions.
- Measurement: define OKRs and measure impact on SLOs and error budget over 90 days post-rollout.
- Completion: if ROI > threshold (reduces error budget burn by X% or reduces p99 latency by Y ms), mark done and update runbooks.

Examples of typical RIs:
- KV-cache hot shard mitigation to reduce p99 latency for long-context models.
- Improved batching and dynamic pad reduction to cut token GPU time by 18%.
- Kernel selection improvements for quantized runs to reduce memory pressure.
- Automated canary analysis tooling to detect quality regressions that surface as server-side errors.

5) Incident review standards and timeline

Triage and timeline:
- Sev classification: Sev-1 (service down or SLA violated for enterprise customer), Sev-2 (degraded but partial functionality), Sev-3 (minor impact).
- Initial incident post: within 30 minutes of declaration by incident commander.
- Preliminary incident review (chronology + short RCA hypothesis): within 72 hours.
- Full postmortem + action plan: within 7 business days for Sev-1/Sev-2, 14 days for Sev-3.
- Owners assigned for each action with due dates and verification criteria.

Postmortem content checklist:
- Incident summary and impact (customers, regions, estimated error budget consumed).
- Timeline of events and commands run.
- Root cause analysis and evidence (logs, traces, dashboards).
- Contributing factors and why detection/mitigation failed or was slow.
- Corrective actions (short-term, medium-term, long-term) with owners and dates.
- Verification plan: how the fix will be validated and when it will be closed.

Blamelessness and communication:
- All incident reviews follow a blameless approach; focus on system/process improvements.
- Customer-facing communications must be coordinated by Customer Success and Product after SRE confirms technical details.

6) Operational tooling and dashboards

Minimum tooling stack:
- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex (long-term) with ingestion of latency, errors, QPS, GPU metrics.
- Dashboards: Grafana folders per service (inference-gateway, model-executor, kv-cache, control-plane). Each dashboard must include p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, QPS, and a compute utilization panel.
- Traces: Jaeger/OpenTelemetry traces with auto-instrumentation for request path.
- Logs: Elastic + Loki centralized logs with structured JSON fields: request_id, model_id, customer_id, route, duration_ms, error_code.
- Alerting: Alertmanager with tiered channels (pager for Sev-1/2, slack for Sev-2/3 monitoring).
- Synthetic tests: Global synthetic agents (us-east1, eu-west1, ap-southeast1) and per-customer internal synthetics for Dedicated.
- Canary analysis: automated canary tool that computes rolling impact on SLIs for any new rollout.

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- P99 latency breach: firing when p99 > 1.2x SLO for 5m sustained (pager for on-call).
- Error rate increase: 5xx rate > 3x baseline for 3m (pager).
- Error budget burn: Rolling 1d burn rate > 2.0 (notify SRE lead + slack channel).
- GPU memory pressure: node GPU mem usage > 85% for 10m (ops slack, on-call).

7) Canonical runbooks (examples)

Runbook: High p99 latency on Hosted Generate API
- Symptoms: Sudden p99 latency increase by >50% and error rate > 0.1% above baseline.
- Initial checks (first 10 minutes):
  1) Confirm alert on Grafana.
  2) Check synthetic agents for region-specific vs global impact.
  3) Query Prometheus: top routes by latency, top model_ids by latency, and 5xx rate.
  4) Inspect recent rollouts (past 60m) via rollout service UI.
- Mitigations (fast):
  - If rollout is suspect: pause and rollback canary.
  - If single model family impacted: route traffic to fallback model variant and scale up healthy pools.
  - If resource pressure: scale GPU pool (launch warm instances) and relieve scheduling by draining non-critical pods.
- Post-incident: open an RI if root cause is systemic (e.g., KV-cache hot shard). Document remediation and update the runbook.

Runbook: Model load failures (OOM or model artifact corruption)
- Symptoms: Model-host process restarts, 5xx on model load endpoints, or failed healthchecks.
- Initial checks:
  1) Inspect node logs for OOM kills and kernel OOM messages.
  2) Verify artifact checksum and size in object storage.
  3) Check GPU memory reservation and model quantization profile.
- Mitigations:
  - If OOM: reduce concurrency, restart pool with increased instance type, and temporarily disable large-model routing.
  - If artifact corruption: restore artifact from last known good checksum and clear cached artifacts on hosts.

8) Runbook hygiene and ownership

- Every runbook must have an owner and a last-reviewed date. Reviews are quarterly.
- Runbook changes must include a short summary and verification steps.
- After any incident where a runbook is used, the owner must submit a short note: what worked, what failed, and required edits within 3 business days.

9) Documentation and references

- Runbooks directory: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks (link: see related_pages).
- Capacity dashboards: Grafana -> Eng-SRE -> Capacity Planning.
- Canary tooling: internal-canary-service README and API docs.
- On-call rota and escalation: Eng-SRE -> oncall-and-incident-response.

Appendix: Quick checklists

Incident quick checklist (first 15 minutes):
1. Acknowledge alert and declare incident severity.
2. Assign incident commander and communication lead.
3. Gather immediate impact (customers affected, regions, error budget consumed).
4. Apply rapid mitigation (pause rollout, failover to region/fallback model).
5. Post initial incident note in incident channel and update status page if required.

Capacity quick checklist (monthly):
1. Export QPS and utilization for last 30 days.
2. Validate reserved Dedicated commitments for next 90 days.
3. Run autoscaler simulation for forecasted peak.
4. Schedule procurement or pool reconfiguration if shortfall > 10%.

Contact and escalation
